id: How to Write a Poem in a Time of War

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You can’t begin just anywhere. It’s a wreck. Shrapnel and the eye Of a house, a row of houses. There’s a rat scrambling From light with fleshy trash in its mouth. A baby strapped to its mother’s back Cut loose. Soldiers crawl the city, The river, the town, the village, The bedroom, our kitchen. They eat everything. Or burn it. They kill what they cannot take. They rape. What they cannot kill they take. Rumors fall like rain. Like bombs. Like mother and father tears swallowed for restless peace. Like sunset slanting toward a moonless midnight. Like a train blown free of its destination. Like a seed fallen where There is no chance of trees or anyplace for birds to live.No, start here. Deer peer from the edge of the woods. We used to see woodpeckers The size of the sun, redbirds, and were greeted By chickadees with their good morning songs. We’d started to cook outside slippery with dew and laughter, ah those smoky sweet sunrises. We tried to pretend war wasn’t going to happen. Though they began building their houses all around us and demanding more. They started teaching our children their god’s story, A story in which we’d always be slaves.No. Not here. You can’t begin here. This is memory shredded because it is impossible to hold by words, even poetry.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- War has devastated homes, families, and entire communities through killing, rape, theft, and destruction.
- Rumors, grief, and displacement create an atmosphere of relentless fear and uncertainty.
- Memories of wildlife, shared meals, laughter, and peaceful mornings contrast sharply with the violence.
- The community tried to deny the approaching war even as outsiders encroached on their land and imposed beliefs that cast them as slaves.
- The trauma is so fragmented and overwhelming that words, including poetry, cannot fully contain it.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem confronts war, displacement, and colonization through fragmented memories, brutal imagery, and repeated attempts to find where the story should begin. It reveals that violence has shattered both home and memory beyond language’s ability to contain them, underscoring trauma’s profound resistance to coherent narration.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Shrapnel, There

outputs.L1:
You can’t begin just anywhere.

It’s a wreck—  
shrapnel and the eye  
of a house, a row of houses.

There’s a rat scrambling  
from the light, fleshy trash in its mouth.  
A baby, strapped to its mother’s back,  
cut loose.

Soldiers crawl through the city,  
the river, the town, the village,  
the bedroom, our kitchen.

They eat everything.  
Or burn it.  
They kill what they cannot take.  
They rape.  
What they cannot kill, they take.

Rumors fall like rain.  
Like bombs.  
Like a mother’s and father’s tears,  
swallowed for a restless peace.  
Like sunset slanting toward a moonless midnight.  
Like a train blown free of its destination.  
Like a seed fallen where  
there is no chance of trees  
or any place for birds to live.

No, start here.

Deer peer from the edge of the woods.  
We used to see woodpeckers  
the size of the sun, redbirds,  
and we were greeted by chickadees  
with their good-morning songs.

We’d started cooking outside,  
slippery with dew and laughter—  
ah, those smoky-sweet sunrises.

We tried to pretend war wasn’t going to happen,  
though they began building their houses all around us  
and demanding more.

They started teaching our children their god’s story,  
a story in which we would always be slaves.

No. Not here.  
You can’t begin here.

This is memory, shredded  
because it is impossible to hold  
in words, even poetry.
outputs.L2:
There is no clear place to start. Everything lies ruined: metal fragments, the hollow window of one home, then an entire line of homes. A rat darts away from brightness, carrying soft human refuse between its teeth. An infant, once tied to its mother’s back, has been severed from her. Troops move through every space—the city and river, the town and village, the bedroom and our kitchen. They consume or set fire to whatever they find. Anything they cannot steal, they destroy; they violate people, and those they do not murder, they seize. Rumors pour down like storms and explosives, like parents’ grief forced inward for the sake of an uneasy calm. They resemble daylight sinking into a night without a moon, a train blasted away from its intended route, or a seed landing in soil where no forest can grow and no birds can make a home.

No—begin somewhere else.

At the forest boundary, deer watch cautiously. Once, we saw enormous woodpeckers, bright as the sun, along with cardinals, while chickadees welcomed us with morning calls. We had begun preparing food outdoors, damp with dew and full of laughter—those dawns fragrant with smoke and sweetness. We acted as though war might never arrive, even while outsiders raised homes on every side of us and kept insisting on more. They taught our children the account of their deity, a narrative that assigned us permanent bondage.

No—not there either. That cannot be the beginning. Memory has been torn into pieces because language cannot contain it, not even the language of poetry.
outputs.L3:
War has devastated homes, torn families apart, and shattered entire communities. Its violence is felt not only in killing, but also in rape, theft, displacement, and the destruction of everything people once relied upon for safety and belonging. Rumors of further attacks spread quickly, deepening the grief of those who have already lost loved ones. Forced from their homes and uncertain of what will happen next, survivors live in an atmosphere of relentless fear.

Against this devastation stand memories of a different life: wildlife moving through the landscape, families sharing meals, children laughing, and peaceful mornings filled with familiar sounds. These recollections make the present violence even more painful. They evoke a world of connection and ordinary joy that has been violently interrupted.

For a time, the community tried to deny that war was approaching. Yet outsiders continued to encroach upon their land, bringing beliefs and systems that treated local people as inferior and sought to reduce them to the status of slaves. By the time the danger could no longer be ignored, fear and destruction had already begun to overwhelm daily life.

The resulting trauma is fragmented, chaotic, and almost impossible to express. Memory arrives in broken images—of loss, tenderness, terror, and vanished peace—rather than as a clear or orderly story. Words can bear witness to what happened, but they cannot fully contain the scale of the suffering. Even poetry, with all its emotional power, reaches its limits before an experience so devastating.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts war, displacement, and colonization by refusing to present them as a clear, orderly history. Instead, it moves through fragmented memories, abrupt images, and repeated attempts to decide where the story should begin. This uncertainty is not simply a stylistic choice; it reflects the speaker’s traumatic experience. War has broken the ordinary sequence of time, making it difficult to distinguish beginnings from endings or memory from the present. Each possible starting point leads back to another act of violence, another loss, or an earlier history of dispossession.

The poem’s brutal imagery emphasizes the physical consequences of conflict while also suggesting the destruction of emotional and cultural life. Bodies, homes, landscapes, and family histories are all marked by violence. Home no longer functions as a secure place of belonging. It has been invaded, damaged, or left behind, and it survives only in incomplete recollections. Displacement therefore becomes more than a geographical condition: the speaker is also displaced from a stable sense of identity, history, and language.

Colonization deepens this rupture by showing that the violence is not limited to a single event. The speaker’s personal suffering is connected to a broader history in which land, culture, and memory have been controlled or erased. The poem’s fractured structure mirrors this history of interruption. Its gaps and repetitions suggest that the past cannot be recovered as a unified narrative because colonial and military violence have destroyed the conditions that would make such coherence possible.

The repeated search for a beginning ultimately reveals the limits of storytelling itself. The speaker wants to testify—to give shape to suffering and preserve what has been lost—but language repeatedly proves inadequate. Words can name certain images or events, yet they cannot fully contain the terror, grief, and disorientation of trauma. As a result, the poem does not resolve its fragments into a complete account. Its broken form becomes its most truthful form of expression, demonstrating that some experiences resist explanation precisely because they have shattered the structures through which people normally understand and narrate their lives.
outputs.L5:
**You, Shrapnel, There**

You stood there after the silence,  
with shrapnel glittering in the street  
like pieces of a broken constellation.

I called your name,  
but distance had already changed it—  
made it smaller, stranger,  
something the wind could carry away.

There are wounds no one can see,  
fragments that remain beneath the skin:  
a voice, a doorway,  
the last look before leaving.

And still, you were there—  
not unbroken, not unafraid,  
but alive enough to turn toward me  
and take one careful step home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about war, displacement, colonial violence, and the impossibility of capturing traumatic memory in words. Use fragmented imagery, repetition, and several false starts about where the story should begin.
counterfactuals.output:
Begin with the border—

no.

Begin with the orchard  
before the uniforms renamed it.

No, begin with the ship,  
its hold full of breath  
counted as cargo.

Begin with the map.

No—

the hand above the map,  
the clean fingernail drawing a line  
through a river,  
through a village,  
through the blue bowl  
where a child was drinking.

This is where the story begins:

with a door unhinged,  
a key cooling in a pocket,  
the house walking backward  
into smoke.

This is where the story—

No.

There was a language for bread.  
There was a language for rain.  
There was a word grandmothers used  
when calling everyone home.

The soldiers took the radio.  
The governor took the names.  
The schoolbook said discovered,  
said pacified,  
said empty land.

Empty, empty—

except for the graves,  
except for the wells stopped with stones,  
except for the mouths  
still shaping forbidden syllables.

Begin with the road, then:

mattress tied to a roof,  
photographs under a shirt,  
one shoe in the ditch,  
one shoe continuing.

At the checkpoint  
a mother opens her bag:

soap,  
salt,  
a spoon bent like a question,  
the deed to a house  
now occupied by someone else’s certainty.

How do I write the gunshot?

Not bang.

Not thunder.

Not anything the alphabet  
has agreed to carry.

It was the sound of a future  
being shut in another room.

It was—

No.

Words arrive afterward,  
late officials  
with clipboards.

They measure the ash.  
They number the missing.  
They ask the wound  
to state its date of birth.

But memory will not stand in line.

Memory is a wall  
with heat still inside it.

Memory is a child waking  
with dirt in her teeth.

Memory is the sea repeating  
no body, no body, no body  
while returning a shirt.

Begin again.

Begin with empire  
calling theft a treaty,  
calling hunger policy,  
calling the cage protection,  
calling the dead unfortunate.

Begin with the flag  
raised over a courthouse  
built from the stones  
of dismantled homes.

No—

begin smaller:

a cup left on a table,  
tea darkening,  
flies at the rim,  
someone saying  
I will be back before—

Before.

Before is a country  
no map admits.

We live there at night.  
We plant the old songs there.  
We speak to those whose faces  
blur at the edges,  
not because they are forgotten  
but because remembering  
has become a kind of fire.

I could tell you—

No, I could not.

I could place each word  
like a white stone  
along the road,

but the road has been renamed.

I could say exile,  
but exile does not limp.

I could say massacre,  
but the word has no temperature.

I could say home,  
home,  
home—

and still not give you  
the window breaking inward,  
the boot in the flour,  
the small red sweater  
caught on the wire.

So let the poem fail.

Let it stutter at the border.  
Let it lose its papers.  
Let it carry what it cannot declare:

a fistful of soil,  
three names,  
a key without a door,  
a door without a wall,  
a wall without—

Begin there.

No.

Begin anywhere.

The wound has no beginning  
that words can reach,

and no ending  
they can close.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a haunting prose poem narrated by someone remembering the destruction of their home and community by soldiers. Contrast graphic scenes of violence with peaceful memories of birds, woods, outdoor cooking, and family life.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the soldiers came, the mornings belonged to birds. Thrushes stitched silver notes between the pines, and blackbirds worried the wet leaves for worms. My mother cooked outside beneath the walnut tree, turning flatbread on a blackened iron while smoke climbed gently through the branches. My father split wood. My sisters carried water, spilling half of it in their laughter. Even the dogs slept without fear.

I remember this because afterward there were other sounds: boots crushing the garden fence, rifle fire cracking open the noon, windows bursting inward like startled wings. A man fell across the well with his hands still cupped around his mouth. In the lane, blood ran through flour from a torn sack, making a pink paste beneath the soldiers’ soles. The school burned first. Then the houses. Then the old women’s shawls caught sparks as they fled.

But before that, in summer, we roasted peppers over coals. Their skins blistered sweetly, and my uncle sang off-key while the children chased fireflies along the wood’s dark edge. We ate with our fingers. We passed salt from hand to hand. Beyond us, the forest breathed its green breath, deep and untroubled.

Years later, I still wake smelling smoke. I see the orchard hacked down, trunks bleeding pale sap. I see my brother beside the wall, his shirt opened by bullets, his face turned toward the hills as if listening for someone calling him home. I see the soldiers laughing near the overturned table where our supper cooled among shards of blue crockery.

And still, impossibly, the birds return in memory. They land on the roof that is no longer there. My mother lifts bread from the iron. My father raises his axe and pauses, smiling at something I have said. The woods stand whole behind them. Evening gathers us close.

Then a gunshot passes through the years.

The birds rise all at once, blackening the sky, and everyone I loved disappears beneath their wings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental anti-war poem that begins with “You can’t begin just anywhere,” includes the refrain “No,” and ends by questioning whether trauma can ever be held by language or poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
You can’t begin just anywhere,  
not with the medal, not with the map,  
not with the clean blue arrow  
crossing a border like a sentence  
certain of its verb.

Begin with the shoe in the road.  
Begin with the road no longer road.  
Begin with a mother dialing  
a number that rings  
inside a crater.

No,

the broadcast says *precision*  
while the window learns  
a new grammar of glass.

No,

the general folds the country  
into a pocket square.  
The dead refuse the crease.

A drone hums above the alphabet.  
A child writes:

H is for home.  
H is for—  
H is  
H

No,

do not call the smoke collateral.  
Do not give the wound  
a bureaucratic coat  
and ask it to stand at attention.

Night enters without papers.  
Names cross out of bodies.  
Somewhere, a soldier washes  
another soldier’s blood  
from a photograph of summer.

No,

there is no after,  
only a clock with shrapnel hands,  
only the door rehearsing  
the knock that already came.

We gather the fragments—  
boot, button, tooth, lullaby—  
and place them in the mouth  
of this poem.

But the mouth is small.  
The silence is not.

Can language hold what war has broken,  
can poetry carry trauma without breaking it again?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented literary monologue about an Indigenous community facing invasion, cultural erasure, and forced religious teaching. Juxtapose nature imagery and joyful mornings with escalating occupation, enslavement, and war.
counterfactuals.output:
Morning once arrived laughing.

Mist lifted from the river in pale ribbons; kingfishers broke the surface like blue sparks. Children ran barefoot between the houses, carrying baskets, carrying jokes, carrying nothing because nothing had yet been taken. Grandmother crushed leaves between her palms and named the medicines. I repeated each word.

The words tasted of rain.

Then sails appeared—

white wounds on the horizon.

At first, we watched. We offered water. We pointed toward the safe channel through the reef. They held up polished metal, bright as captured sunlight, and smiled with all their teeth.

Behind them came more.

More hulls. More flags. More men measuring the shore with ropes, measuring our fields, measuring even the silence between our names.

They drove posts into the earth.

This belongs to the Crown, they said.

The earth did not answer.

Or perhaps it answered in roots, in the shudder of cedar boughs, in the sudden flight of birds. Perhaps we had forgotten how loudly the world can refuse.

*

Morning still arrived laughing.

That was the cruelty of it.

The orchids opened. Fish flashed silver beneath the canoes. Somewhere a girl sang while grinding grain, and for one breath the village was whole.

Then the bell rang.

Not our drum. Not our shell horn.

Their bell.

They gathered the children beneath a roof that smelled of damp wool and punishment. Your old names are heathen, they said. Your stories are lies. They washed our tongues with ash, dressed our sons in stiff cloth, cut our daughters’ hair, placed a book before them and called it mercy.

Repeat after me.

Repeat.

After.

Me.

I watched my little brother move his lips around a foreign heaven while our ancestors waited outside in the rain.

*

They burned the carved house first.

They said the figures were devils.

They burned the masks, the baskets woven with river-patterns, the blankets where our histories crossed in red and black. Smoke carried generations upward. Ash settled on the soldiers’ shoulders like gray snow.

They did not notice.

Or they thought it blessing.

Grandmother knelt in the ruins and gathered charcoal in her hands.

Remember, she told me.

But memory had become contraband.

*

The fields changed.

Where we planted food, they planted fences.

Where we buried our dead, they built a road.

Where the deer came at dusk, horses dragged cannon wheels through mud.

Men were taken to cut timber for forts. Women were made to cook in houses raised from stolen trees. Children hauled stone until their hands split. They called it labor, tribute, civilization.

We called it by the names of those who did not return.

*

Still, dawn—

gold poured over the eastern ridge.

For a moment every musket barrel shone like a reed wet with dew.

For a moment the occupied shore was beautiful.

I hated the sun for touching them and us alike.

*

We fled inland.

We carried seeds in pouches beneath our clothes. We carried embers in clay bowls. We carried the forbidden words, whispering them into infants’ ears so softly even the priests could not hear.

River.

Heron.

Mother.

Home.

Behind us, the fort grew.

Then another.

Then another.

The map filled with their names.

Our country became blank space beneath their ink.

*

War did not begin with a battle.

It began with a fence.

A sermon.

A missing child.

A boot in the garden.

A hand closing around a wrist.

It began each morning when we woke and found the world still ours in memory, theirs by decree.

Then came the rifles in the cane grass.

The torches moving at night.

The drums answering from hill to hill—not celebration now, but warning.

I saw boys who once raced dragonflies paint their faces for war. I saw mothers sharpen blades beside sleeping babies. I saw elders stand where the path narrowed, their white hair bright in the dawn.

The bell rang.

Our drums replied.

*

Do not say we vanished.

The river remembers our true names. The mountains keep the shape of our songs. Beneath the chapel floor, beneath the governor’s road, beneath the fields where chained hands harvested wealth for strangers, our footprints remain pressed into the older earth.

And every morning—

even now—

birds lift from the reeds.

Children laugh somewhere beyond the fence.

A grandmother bends close, leaf crushed between her palms.

Listen, she says.

Repeat after me.

Not their prayer.

Ours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a bleak, nonlinear poem in which a survivor struggles to decide where to begin recounting war. Include ruined houses, fleeing animals, soldiers, rumors compared to rain and bombs, nostalgic woodland birds, settlers building nearby, and memory described as shredded.
counterfactuals.output:
**Where to Begin**

Begin with the roof already gone,  
the rooms holding weather  
instead of children.

No—begin later:

soldiers rinsing their hands  
in a ditch where the moon  
had been broken into coins.

Or earlier, when rumors fell  
like rain—soft at first,  
then everywhere—  
and afterward like bombs,  
each one opening  
a black mouth in the earth.

The animals knew.

Dogs fled without barking.  
Cattle tore through fences.  
A fox crossed the road at noon,  
its red body carrying  
the last clear warning.

Years before, woodland birds  
stitched morning to morning—  
thrush, cuckoo, the small brown ones  
whose names my mother knew.  
I hear them now only as nostalgia,  
calling from trees that survived  
in no country I can reach.

Begin with the ruined houses.  
Begin with the cups still upright  
under ash.  
Begin with the dead.

No. They have been made  
to begin too often.

Nearby, settlers raise walls,  
measure gardens, hammer bright roofs  
into the wounded distance.  
Their children sleep  
where ours learned to run.

My memory is shredded—  
cloth caught on wire,  
a map gnawed by fire,  
sentences without roads between them.

So I begin at the end:

I lived.

This is not triumph.  
It is only the place  
where the telling fails,  
and fails again,  
and must begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
